Torridon is one of three areas where the Our Rainforest Futures project aims to restore woodlands

Almost £6m has been given to a five-year project set up to restore Scotland's rare rainforest.

The award from the National Lottery Heritage Fund will support the creation of three hubs to be located in Torridon, Morvern and mid-Argyll.

Through the Our Rainforest Futures project local people will be given training and work opportunities around habitat restoration, deer management and the removal of invasive species.

About 75,000 acres (30,351ha) of rain-soaked woodlands on the west coast are designated Atlantic rainforest because of the rare oceanic plant life.

Rare species found in Scotland's declining rainforest

When Amazon leaders blessed Scotland's rainforest

The forest has been found to be home to hundreds of species including glow worms, slime moulds and rare lichens.

Overgrazing by deer and livestock, invasive plant species and disease are among the threats to the surviving areas of woodland.

The Torridon hub would involve communities in Kinlochewe, Shieldaig, Lochcarron, Applecross and Gairloch.

In Morvern, the project would include Lochaline, Strontian and Tobermory in Mull.

Mid-Argyll's hub would involve communities Crinan, Tayvallich, Lochgilphead, Ardrishaig and Tarbert.

Tobermory on Mull is among communities that will be asked to be involved in mid-Argyll

Our Rainforest Futures is an Alliance for Scotland's Rainforest project led by the Woodland Trust Scotland.

Argyll Countryside Trust, Community Woodlands Association, Plantlife, RSPB Scotland and SRUC are involved.

Caroline Clark, Scotland director of The National Lottery Heritage Fund, said Scotland's rainforest was internationally significant but largely unknown.

She said: "A 2025 survey found fewer than one in three people even know it exists.

"This major investment, using funds raised by National Lottery players, recognises that the future of our rainforest and the future of many west coast communities are closely linked. With the right support, both can thrive."

Julie Stoneman, Saving Scotland's Rainforest Programme manager at the charity Plantlife, said it was hoped the project could create more than 20 jobs and 15 trainee posts.

MN202611_delbywhbcm.t:
England head coach Thomas Tuchel used long-time first choice Jordan Pickford (left) and James Trafford (right) during the previous international break

When England head coach Thomas Tuchel decided to pick Leeds United goalkeeper James Trafford to face World Cup holders Spain at Wembley in the last international break, it sparked the first stirrings about preparations for life without long-time first choice Jordan Pickford.

Tuchel made it clear Pickford was still England's number one pick, but the simple fact he decided to alternate keepers - playing Trafford in the 3-2 loss to Spain then victory against Czech Republic, before Everton's 32-year-old returned for the Wembley win against the Czechs and the 7-0 rout in Croatia - created intrigue and debate.

England meet Croatia at Wembley on Thursday before facing the biggest test of their Uefa Nations League campaign when they play Spain in Madrid on Sunday.

Tuchel maintains strong faith in Pickford, an outstanding performer for England, but Trafford has at least had the chance to stake his claim.

Tuchel has suggested he may use a rotation system for the pair once more in the upcoming internationals, which will only increase scrutiny on England's goalkeeping position.

Pickford's record is outstanding since he made his debut in a 0-0 draw against Germany at Wembley in 2017.

In his time as first choice, England have once more emerged as major players on global stage, reaching the World Cup semi-finals in 2018 and 2026, as well as successive Euros finals at the delayed 2020 tournament and Euro 2024.

Measured by Opta stats, Pickford has made only two errors leading to goals in 93 appearances, with 46 clean sheets and a 74% save ratio.

Trafford's international career is in its infancy and, while former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson says Pickford remains Tuchel's undisputed first choice, he believes the head coach's recent strategy is a sensible one.

Robinson told BBC Sport: "It obviously remains to be seen what Thomas Tuchel does in these two England games, but I could see exactly what he was doing by giving James Trafford game time in the last round of matches.

"We are so guilty as a nation of taking one goalkeeper to a tournament who has 70, 80, 90 caps, then the two of three below him could have less than double figures combined."

Robinson's point is proved by the statistic that 80 of Pickford's appearances have been competitive games, with 33 at major tournaments, made up of 19 at the World Cup and 14 at European Championships.

"Competitive and tournament caps give you the type of experience you can't get as a number two or three keeper," said Robinson.

"James Trafford is only 24 and has four caps - two of them competitive - so you can see exactly what Tuchel is doing, looking ahead to a situation where England's recognised number one is not available to him, or there is a drop off in form.

"We saw the last selections and all thought Jordan Pickford's place is under threat and James Trafford is going to be the next number one. I don't think Thomas Tuchel saw it as starkly or simply as that.

"It's a conversation that will definitely take place down the road, but not now. Jordan is England's first choice, in my opinion, rightfully so given his consistency and performances over such a long period.

"This is a debate and conversation for the future definitely because Father Time catches up with everyone eventually and the manager needs to have a contingency plan, but Jordan Pickford very much remains number one and Thomas Tuchel has said as much.

"I don't think Jordan Pickford is under threat for his jersey on a permanent basis any time soon, irrespective of the next selection, but what Tuchel is doing reinforces the impression that he has to be at the top of his game and maintain high standards, which he certainly has been doing when I've watched him this season.

"The biggest compliment I can pay Jordan Pickford is that when you have got that England goalkeeper's shirt, everybody thinks somebody else should be doing it. I know that from personal experience.

"You're there to be shot at, but there has been no noise around Jordan Pickford for a very long time now.

"It has worked both ways for Jordan, James and Thomas Tuchel, and worked very well. Jordan knows he can't rest on his laurels and he will just play regardless. He has to be playing well.

"Is James Trafford challenging Jordan Pickford right now? Yes he is - if Jordan Pickford isn't playing very well and Jordan Pickford is making errors.

"None of the above are true right now because he's playing well for Everton and has done nothing wrong for England."

Robinson also drew on club form to support Pickford's case. Since the start of the 2024-25 season, only Arsenal's title-winning keeper David Raya has more clean sheets in the league than Pickford at Everton.

Raya has 39 clean sheets in that time, while Pickford has 27, with Robinson saying: "That's a superb record and all logic tells you Pickford will have to work a lot harder for his clean sheets than David Raya."

Trafford staked his claim in those Nations League games against Spain and the Czech Republic, putting him at the forefront of Tuchel's thoughts as the main understudy to Pickford.

Crystal Palace's Dean Henderson is now back in contention after injury and hoping to add to his six caps, although he has not been included in Tuchel's latest squad.

Trafford moved to Leeds United from Manchester City in the summer in a British record deal for a goalkeeper that could be worth up to £45m.

It came after a £23m move to City from Burnley the previous summer, when his hopes of becoming Pep Guardiola's first choice were unexpectedly ended by the decision to sign Gianluigi Donnarumma from Paris St-Germain.

Robinson said: "James Trafford needed that move to Leeds United and Leeds United needed a keeper of his level. This is a match made in heaven.

"And don't forget, in a Premier League career with Burnley, Manchester City and Leeds United, Trafford has only played 42 Premier League games – just a little more than a full season – and one Champions League game. He needs this experience.

"He's got a huge amount of potential, with his quality, all-round goalkeeping and mental approach. He has the potential be England's future number one, which Tuchel clearly sees him to be.

"He has the mentality to reach the very top, which is very difficult because not all goalkeepers have that. It's a tough place to be, a very lonely place to be, but he has the ability to cope with that situation.

"I was at Bournemouth when he made an error in the Leeds United defeat there, but, knowing the type of character he, is it won't faze him. It won't bother him. Because of his personality and his character traits, he has got the ability to go right to the top.

"You'd think Dean Henderson will be back in the squad in due course once he has played more games.

"Jason Steele is in there again, but he's a mentor figure behind the scenes, not someone who will ever start or threaten the established goalkeepers.

"If you rewind back 18 or 24 months, you had Nick Pope, Sam Johnstone, James Trafford, Dean Henderson, Aaron Ramsdale and Jordan Pickford - a real plethora of England goalkeepers.

"Now Nick Pope is not playing at Newcastle United, Sam Johnstone's not in the equation and Aaron Ramsdale is nowhere near."

Ramsdale's decline has been dramatic after leaving Arsenal for Southampton in August 2024, with a loan spell at Newcastle United proving to be unsuccessful. He has effectively been fourth choice at Saints this season, failing to make matchday squads.

Robinson said: "I find Aaron Ramsdale's situation very sad because I believe he's a goalkeeper able to play at the top level.

"He should be in this conversation because he's a goalkeeper I really like, but he's been very unfortunate with selection of clubs and the way their season have gone. I still think there is time for him to come back into the reckoning.

"For now, though, if there is a conversation to be had about England's goalkeepers, then Jordan Pickford and James Trafford is that conversation, with Jordan still very much the number one right now as far as I'm concerned."

MN202611_9xz50rs1hl.t:
Phil Lambert said painting with soil was "something I've been very familiar with"

An artist has set a record for the world's largest soil painting as he bids to raise awareness of how important the material is.

The UK-based Official Record Breakers has verified that organisation Save Soil had surpassed the previous best of 59,458 sq cm (about 64 sq ft), with the new painting measuring 61,000 sq cm (about 65 sq ft).

Phil Lambert, who lives in Cardiff, used four types of soil and an upcycled wooden frame and canvas supplied by Oxford Wood Recycling.

The artwork was created to raise awareness of the movement's call for soil regeneration to be prioritised at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP).

Save Soil is pushing for improvement of soil health around the world and works with governments to shape policies on the subject.

The painting, which Lambert created at University College London (UCL), follows its new report, which outlines the importance of healthy soils and steps for their restoration.

The artist used a mix of soil from various sources

Lambert said he had been using soil for about 10 years and painting with it "is something I've been very familiar with".

As well as using soil from his garden and some from his mother's home, the artist also received donations from the James Hutton Institute in Scotland.

"I did have a motive in my mind of this tree and hedge and field," he said.

Through his work with scientists, Lambert said he had been taught about the "perils and the needs of soil".

"If you go back to the fields you were walking in when you were young, you will notice that there is a thinner soil on there and there's more rock on the surface," he said.

Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire

UK Save Soil spokesperson Henry Asplin called the painting "a visual call to action".

"Soil is the planet's quiet infrastructure and one of our greatest climate solutions, yet it remains largely invisible in national climate plans," he said.

Mark Maslin, climate scientist and professor at UCL, said healthy soils "regulate water, store carbon, and underpin biodiversity and food systems".

"...protecting and restoring soil must sit at the heart of every nation's climate strategy if we are serious about limiting warming and securing a liveable future," he added.

Climate scientist Mark Maslin (left) called the painting "a powerful reminder that protecting and restoring soil must sit at the heart of every nation's climate strategy"

Jennifer Robinson, from Abingdon-based Oxford Wood Recycling, said looking after the environment was "at the heart" of its work.

She said the company collected wood from several sites across Oxfordshire.

"I myself come from a farming background, so ... I think [Save Soil]'s cause and what they're trying to do is absolutely crucial," she said.

Robinson said she had been noticing changes in the colour of soil locally.

"We're all seeing massive cracks as we're out walking and the areas where there are more plants and more trees, the soil is less exposed and evidently healthier."

Jonathan Ross and David Walliams pictured in 2005

TV presenter Jonathan Ross has said he is "horrified" by allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams and the rape conviction of Russell Brand.

In a statement, Ross said he was once "on friendly terms with both men", but that at the time he was "genuinely unaware of their conduct".

ITV News and the Guardian on Tuesday published reports alleging that Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women. Walliams denies all the allegations against him. Brand was sentenced to 10 years in jail for rape on Monday.

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said that the allegations against Walliams were the "latest in a long line of reported abuses of power" in the media.

Some of the women accuse Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers, or allege other inappropriate behaviour.

In a letter to journalists published by the Guardian, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

In his statement, Ross also addressed a joke he made at a comedy awards show in 2004, in which the punchline suggested Walliams would be "going home" with a 15-year-old.

Ross acknowledged the controversial quip and described it as "tasteless".

He added: "This joke was submitted to me by the Comedy Awards script writing team and I believed that the punchline was a reference to the fact he had publicly dated younger women, exaggerated for comic effect.

"Had I had any reason to suspect that it might be referring to actual events, I would not only have refused to use it, but I would not have felt comfortable continuing a personal or professional relationship with him."

Why Walliams' unprecedented legal battle to stay anonymous failed

Ross is one of the country's best-known TV presenters, having regularly hosted celebrities on his Jonathan Ross Show, including David Walliams and Russell Brand.

He said he was "as horrified by the revelations about David Walliams and the crimes of Russell Brand as the rest of the nation".

He added: "My thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward."

One woman alleges she met Walliams at a fan event when she was 15. She says he groomed her and they had sex when she was 17

Another woman alleges she met Walliams for a coffee when she was 15, before going back to his house where he allegedly tried to lift up her shirt and commit an act that she now describes as a sexual assault

A woman who worked as a model in her teens accused Walliams of grooming her. A different woman who also worked as a model said Walliams tried to kiss her while showing her around his home

The investigation claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another

Other women allege inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room

Lilly Creightmore, accusing Walliams of grooming, speaks to BBC Newsnight

In the ITV documentary revealing the allegations, Jonathan Ross is pictured at an event also attended by a woman who later made accusations about the conduct of Walliams.

Ross and Brand were also widely criticised for leaving lewd voicemails for Fawlty Towers actor Andrew Sachs, the grandfather of Georgina Baillie with whom Brand was in a consensual relationship in the mid-2000s, during a BBC Radio 2 broadcast.

Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years' imprisonment for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and the Metropolitan Police has confirmed several people have approached them about the disgraced star since his conviction.

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said on Tuesday: "These allegations are the latest in a long line of reported abuses of power in an industry where we have known for so long that the power imbalances are huge.

"Russell Brand's eventual conviction was a stark reminder that we are still far too reliant on the courage of brave women who choose to come forward despite knowing they will pay a heavy price and may not be believed - and a handful of persistent journalists who risk everything to tell their stories.

"Women must feel safe in their jobs, whistleblowers must be protected, and those who abuse their position must no longer be able to hide behind it."

Downing Street earlier called the allegations "deeply troubling".

Walliams rose to fame alongside Matt Lucas in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent, and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

A BBC spokesperson described the allegations as "serious" and said the corporation has removed Little Britain from BBC iPlayer.

In a further statement released on Wednesday, the BBC said it was "not currently aware of having received any related reports of allegations of sexual misconduct" by Walliams.

"We take allegations of this kind extremely seriously and would encourage anyone with concerns we should be aware of to speak with us."

Several women have spoken to the Guardian and ITV News as part of a joint three-year investigation by the media companies, accusing Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. The investigation was published after Walliams lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public.

One of the women now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault".

David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct after losing injunction bid

Why Walliams' unprecedented legal battle to stay anonymous failed

David Walliams' career and controversies including Britain's Got Talent and Little Britain

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Lilly Creightmore, who has alleged Walliams "groomed" her as a teenager, said she was "angry" at his behaviour.

She said that Walliams invited her to move in with him while she was "in between living situations". She was 18 at the time. She "felt instantly pressured to share a bed with him" but told him she was not interested in him in a romantic way.

After about a week of refusing Walliams's advances, Creightmore said "he started to become very moody and rude and cold".

According to ITV, Walliams says he did not act inappropriately and did not "target" her because she was "vulnerable" or "young".

TV agent Dermot McNamara, who has represented someone allegedly groomed by Walliams, told BBC Newsnight he had informed "authorities and broadcasters" about Walliams's alleged "inappropriate behaviour" but no action was taken.

Walliams denies all allegations, and in a statement to journalists shared by the Guardian said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

He acknowledged that "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with" and said he regretted not always taking "people's feelings properly into account".

Watch: TV agent says no action was taken after he reported alleged 'inappropriate behaviour' by David Walliams

The Metropolitan Police have since contacted the Guardian and ITV News "to ensure that any potential victims" are "made aware of how they could report any criminal allegations to police".

A spokesperson added: "The Met has not received any related reports of sexual assault or any other offences. Should we receive any reports, they will be carefully assessed."

Comedian Lucy Beaumont told Sky News on Tuesday that she was one of the people who spoke to the Guardian about allegations raised with her about Walliams.

A young TV worker had approached Beaumont about concerns of Walliams engaging in inappropriate behaviour with "young girls" who were "definitely" older than 16, the comedian said.

The young person said he had worked on a programme involving Walliams where he was tasked with taking the "young girls" to Walliams's dressing room, adding: "He felt they were vulnerable."

What we know about the allegations against David Walliams

Beaumont said she reached out to an alleged victim who was "in a really bad way" and was worried about her well-being but said the woman "declined my offer of support".

The 43-year-old comedian said she had never worked with Walliams or witnessed any inappropriate behaviour from him but was "worried that these girls were very young".

She believes there is not a robust "duty of care" to protect people within the TV industry from sexual misconduct nor an adequate reporting system for whistleblowers.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday, Labour MP Jess Phillips said: "We shouldn't always look for a criminal threshold in all these cases."

The former secretary of state for safeguarding violence against women and girls said: "If you compare the David Walliams story with the Russell Brand story, there is a clear blue water between, one is a criminal case, one is a series of allegations... but the behaviour needs to be stopped.

"What is described in the David Walliams story is an absolute modus operandi, a target group of women of a certain age, the kind of women who don't have the same amount of power as if you were doing this to a 35-year-old woman who might have a bit more about herself in the world. And so they're targeting a group of people and they are looking at what they can get away with."

She described the allegations, which Walliams denies, as "dangerous behaviour" which "leads to so much abuse in our society".

"Whether criminal exploitation or sexual exploitation, that I think we need to look at grooming much more closely in the round."

In his statement to ITV News and the Guardian, Walliams said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

An artist's rendering of Trump's proposed arch near Arlington Cemetery

The family of former US President John F Kennedy has sued to block construction of a triumphal arch that President Donald Trump plans to build in the nation's capital.

Nine members of the political dynasty argue the 250ft (76m) structure would block the view of Kennedy's grave, as well as the graves of thousands of veterans buried at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia.

Last week, a US judge temporarily halted the project on the heels of a vote allowing construction to proceed.

The White House said it was "unfortunate" to see that some members of the Kennedy family had joined litigation against an arch "intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery".

"The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis R Ingle said in a statement to the BBC.

"We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds," he added.

Watch: Protesters demonstrate against Trump’s proposed arch

Last week the project won approval from the National Capital Planning Commission.

But US District Judge Tanya Chutkan then ruled there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch as litigation plays out.

The Kennedy family filed its complaint under a joint lawsuit brought by the state of Virginia and Washington DC seeking to block construction, arguing that the arch will damage "historically significant sightlines" if erected at the gateway of the cemetery.

The plaintiffs include seven children of Robert and Ethel Kennedy, as well as their grandson - former Democrat congressman Joe Kennedy - and Ted Kennedy's son Edward Kennedy Jr.

It does not include Trump cabinet official Robert F Kennedy Jr, who leads the Department of Health and Human Services.

Their motion moves to intervene in two other lawsuits filed by conservationists and veterans seeking to halt the construction.

They say the arch would be a "permanent denigration" of the gravesites and that the Kennedy offspring "would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended".

The Kennedy family argues the structure "will permanently cast shadows over and damage historically significant sightlines to the existing gravesites and memorials established in the Kennedy family's honor" at the cemetery.

The structure would also "fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the gravesites", including the memorials of hundreds of thousands of US veterans, the Kennedys said.

The complaint said that the National Park Service and Interior Department authorised construction on 5 November 2026 without the necessary congressional approval.

The so-called Arc de Trump is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.

Last year, he also added his name to the Kennedy Center, a major Washington DC cultural institution named in honour of JFK.

Trump's name remained on the facade for six months until the addition was ruled illegal and removed.

El Salvador's president posted a video on X of the strikes on a complex he said is the headquarters of 400 Mawozo

Haiti's Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé has praised "the commitment of the Salvadorean forces in the fight against gangs" after a joint strike on a house allegedly used by the leader of the 400 Mawozo gang.

El Salvador's President, Nayib Bukele, had earlier announced that a joint task force had "destroyed" what he described as "the house of Lanmò San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters".

A small contingent of Salvadorean troops has been in Haiti since January 2025 as part of a multinational force deployed to suppress gang violence.

Last month, Bukele sent an extra 2,000 soldiers to rescue four Salvadoreans who have been missing since they were ambushed on 18 October.

Bukele's post on X , external was accompanied by video of several helicopters firing on a large complex.

As the helicopters circle above, dozens of people can be seen running out of the property, fleeing the strikes.

Writing in Creole, Bukele said "we kept our promise", adding that the alleged gang members "ran away without even trying to fight".

Local media reported that as many as 20 people were killed in the strike, which they said was carried out in the early hours of Sunday.

They also reported that Lanmò San Jou, whose real name is Wilson Joseph, was not at the property at the time of the attack.

Posting on X on Tuesday, Fils-Aimé thanked the Salvadorean military's commitment "in the fight against gangs" and said the two nations would keep working together, along with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), to "regain control of the territory and restore state authority".

"THE GANGS WILL GET NO SLEEP!" he added.

While he did not provide any further details about the joint operation or the number of casualties, Fils-Aimé posted a still from the video shared by Bukele showing a helicopter firing a projectile at the compound.

The BBC has not been able to verify the video posted by Bukele, nor whether the property is indeed the headquarters of the 400 Mawozo, Haiti's largest criminal gang, which is infamous for carrying out kidnappings for ransom.

Salvadorean troops have become a regular sight in Port-au-Prince

The attack on the alleged gang headquarters seemingly came after a user on X had urged Bukele to attack the complex.

"Where is that house? Give us the exact address, and we'll destroy it," the Salvadorean president replied to the post, which has now been taken down, apparently for violating X's rules.

Bukele has threatened Haitian gangs before.

Following the kidnapping of four Salvadorean air force technicians on 18 October, he addressed "the gang leaders and gang members holding our four compatriots hostage in Haiti" directly.

"We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too," he wrote in Creole, referring to his crackdown on gang violence in his own country.

The four abducted Salvadoreans were working as part of the GSF, made up of troops from several nations.

Bukele's decision to send thousands of additional troops to Haiti since their abduction has raised concerns with critics who say they are not all working within the command structure of the GSF.

It has also raised questions about the operational legitimacy and legality of their actions in the Caribbean nation.

Amnesty International has urged both countries to "ensure all operations conducted by Salvadorean forces in Haiti comply with international human rights law".

A federal judge in Florida has allowed US President Donald Trump's defamation case against the BBC to go ahead after the broadcaster sought to dismiss it.

But Judge Jeffrey Kuntz dismissed a second claim in the $10bn (£7.5bn) lawsuit under the state's unfair trade practices law.

The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Trump called the judge's ruling a "huge victory" in a Truth Social post on Tuesday. A BBC spokesperson said: "We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage."

The BBC spokesperson added: "We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process."

Judge Kuntz found Trump's defamation allegations against the BBC sufficient for the case to continue, although he did not make a ruling on the merits of the case.

"Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day," he wrote in Tuesday's order.

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC apologised and said that the broadcast had given "the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action".

The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

Along with defamation, Trump claimed in the lawsuit that the broadcaster had violated Florida law, specifically the Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

Kuntz on Tuesday dismissed that part of the lawsuit, ruling that the documentary did not constitute commercial speech.

Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit

A judge ordered Trump last month to answer questions under oath in the lawsuit by 11 December, after the president cancelled a previous deposition last month, citing "matters of national importance".

A lawyer representing the BBC said in court that Trump was campaigning in Georgia in October on the scheduled day and had "prioritised that" over answering their questions.

Earlier this year, Trump's lawyers conceded they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally argued - or on the BBC's website, BBC Select or through US broadcasters.

Trump ultimately agreed to drop BBC Studios, the broadcaster's commercial arm, from his defamation lawsuit, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary".

MN202611_10om1wjeydd.t:
The US removed all its bombers from the UK's RAF Fairford base last month after a major incident in September that police described as "suspicious"

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.

The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.

The three men have been accused by the DOJ of being involved in 18 attacks and attempted attacks, including in London, Amsterdam and Paris. Some of the incidents were said to be directed by the men over FaceTime.

The DOJ said they acted in the name of the group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI).

Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.

The DOJ said that most recently, al-Hassani "orchestrated a terrorist plot" at RAF Fairford - where on 27 September a major incident was declared after suspicious vans were reported near the base.

Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident at RAF Fairford.

Iran has strongly denied any involvement.

Al-Hassani and Mohajeri were allegedly both in Iran at the time of the incident, the indictment claims.

Meanwhile, al-Saadi was coordinating with the pair through third parties from a prison in New York, where he is awaiting trial on previous charges after being arrested in August, it adds.

US court records show that al-Saadi is due in court on 19 November, though it is not clear whether this status conference - which is usually a routine scheduled appearance - relates to the new charges or the previous ones. The BBC has asked the Southern District of New York for comment.

Mohammad Ali al-Hassani (left) and Mohsen Mohajeri (right) allegedly planned attacks on London from Iraq

Mohajeri and al-Hassani are not in custody, two sources told the BBC's US partner CBS News.

The BBC has asked the DOJ for comment on the suspected whereabouts of the two men not in US custody.

In the DOJ's statement detailing the indictments, it said: "Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK."

It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen".

Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year.

The indictment also details an arson attack on a Jewish charity in London on 17 April, which allegedly saw al-Hassani "directing" an individual over FaceTime.

On 17 April , a building previously used by Jewish Futures, an educational charity, was set alight in Hendon, north-west London.

The following day, the DOJ said al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London.

On 18 April, Kenton United Synagogue in Harrow was targeted in an arson attack. A 17-year-old boy pleaded guilty to the incident earlier this year.

Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi is currently in prison in New York, awaiting trial for previous charges

The indictment also claims the three were involved in attacks on the Bank of New York Mellon building in Amsterdam on 15 March and on the Bank of America building in Paris on 28 March.

It added that the trio tried to carry out attacks on "Jewish institutions in the US", including attempting to target a synagogue in Manhattan, New York in March or April.

"This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said.

He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention.

Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah.

Armed police officers were posted outside the RAF Fairford base following the incident in September

A major incident was declared on 27 September near the UK's RAF Fairford base, in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase.

No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized.

The DOJ said that in August, al-Hassani "allegedly directed and paid associates" in the UK to "conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford terrorist plot".

On 22 August, al-Hassani paid one individual to "perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford's perimeter", the department said.

In September, al-Hassani paid several people to help him prepare for the plot, the DOJ also alleged.

According to its statement, this included "procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel".

The suspects then gave the vans an appearance of being used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business, the DOJ stated.

"On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base."

The DOJ also said al-Hassani was "in frequent communication" with the van drivers and helped to direct them where to drive.

"At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route," it added.

It was in the very early hours of 27 September, that the vans were spotted by a local farmer who was heading home from a party, and called the police.

The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.

Two British nationals appeared in court last month in connection with the alleged Iran-linked plot.

The US withdrew all its bombers from RAF Fairford after the incident, with President Donald Trump citing "some threats" to the base as the reason.

RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from there to the Middle East for "defensive" strikes on Iran.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

Watch: Republicans vote to block Hegseth impeachment from reaching full vote

An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill.

A majority of the House of Representatives voted to refer impeachment articles to a committee - essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky.

During an earlier briefing, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage".

The bid to find the cabinet secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump.

That calculation might change in January, when the opposition Democratic Party assumes control of both chambers of Congress, following its successes in the US midterm elections. For now, Trump's Republican Party remains in control.

After Tuesday's vote, the most senior Democrat in the House, Hakeem Jeffries, said: "This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning."

The question on which lawmakers were voting on Tuesday was whether or not to refer the resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, which is led by Republicans. The alternative would have been to allow the resolution to proceed in the House itself.

All Republicans other than Massie voted to refer the resolution to the committee, meaning that the congressman's effort failed in a 211-204 vote.

The move to send the measure to the panel effectively kills the effort, as there is only a short period of time left in this Congress.

More than a dozen members missed the ballot. They included 11 Democrats, several of whom blamed traffic issues for their absences.

Several members of the party criticised their fellow lawmakers for missing the vote.

"You should show up and do your job," said Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed during an interview with CNN, making a direct address to those who did not vote. The Michigan lawmaker recently won a US Senate race in Michigan, having criticised US ties to Israel and the war in Iran on the campaign trail.

Analysis: Hegseth fights for his political life with appeal to Trump

Meanwhile Trump celebrated Tuesday's outcome in a post on Truth Social, saying the effort "has miserably FAILED".

"Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot," Trump said, referring to Hegseth.

After the vote, Massie said he "wasn't surprised" but "was disappointed", according to BBC's US media partner CBS.

"My diagnosis of Congress is these people know what to do," he added. "They just can't bring themselves to do it, even when it would benefit them politically."

Massie had previously acknowledged his impeachment bid may not succeed immediately, but argued it could help push Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.

Hegseth: Impeachment effort is "farce" and "stunt"

The Kentucky congressman also said that removing Hegseth now would give the Senate time to approve a replacement while Republicans were still in power.

Impeachment resolutions can be carried past the end of a congressional term, meaning Democrats would be able to take it up next year.

The Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in January following a successful midterm election that allowed them control of both chambers.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, had predicted earlier in the day that the impeachment bid would fail.

In the eight articles of impeachment formally introduced in the House on Monday, Massie said Hegseth was "breaking the law and must be held accountable" for fighting a war in Iran for more than 90 days without lawmakers' approval.

The impeachment articles also accused Hegseth of overseeing "extrajudicial killings" in the US campaign against boats alleged to be carrying drugs in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.

At a news conference on Tuesday, Hegseth called efforts to impeach him a political stunt by a Trump administration opponent who was "disgruntled and defeated".

Hegseth also argued Massie's resolution endangered national security, because it communicated to US adversaries "that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations".

"This is not patriotism. This is sabotage," he said.

He echoed some statements Trump had made during a surprise appearance at the White House briefing room on Monday, including touting a rise in military recruitment levels.

But Hegseth said Massie was motivated by policy differences and "not high crimes, not misdemeanours, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offences the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause".

Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year to a Trump-backed opponent, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it began in February.

He had already incurred the president's ire for demanding the Trump administration release files on deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

While Hegseth has survived politically for now, many lawmakers - including some Republicans - have questioned how long he can last in the administration.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz, a Republican, said on Tuesday he expected Hegseth to resign or be fired by Trump.

Plans to sell land and farms in Devon had already caused upset among tenants on the Duchy estate

Plans by the Prince of Wales to sell off up to 20% of the Duchy of Cornwall could see more tenant farmers across England asked to buy their farms or move out.

Up to 40 farm holdings across Devon, Cornwall, Herefordshire and the Midlands could be affected by the sale, according to the Tenant Farmers Association (TFA).

Locals say talks over the future of nine farms on the Bradninch estate in Devon have already caused "distress" for some tenants who fear they cannot afford to buy.

A spokeswoman said the Duchy could not confirm the total number of tenants affected by the ten-year sale plan , external but told the BBC the estate was "supporting them through the process with care and respect".

The Duchy's rural director Matthew Morris said he was listening to feedback from farmers

The Duchy, which covers around 51,800 hectares (128,000 acres) in 19 counties, plans to use the £500m raised from the property and land sale over the next decade to invest in local communities, affordable housing and environmental projects.

Former GP Mary Ryan, a local Lib Dem councillor who has lived near the Bradninch estate for around 35 years and is supporting the farmers, said some of those affected were "experiencing enormous mental and emotional distress" as a result of the planned sell-off.

She added that while the Duchy had reportedly apologised to tenants last month, the handling of the process had been "pretty dire".

The sales programme has now been extended from Bradninch, near Cullompton, to the Duloe Estate in Cornwall and to individual holdings elsewhere in Cornwall, Herefordshire and the Midlands, according to the TFA.

The Duchy's rural director, Matthew Morris, told the BBC he was listening to feedback over how the sales were being handled and offering support and mental health advice to tenants.

Morris added that the Duchy was "still committed to agriculture" but that there "may well be other disposals in the future".

In terms of immediate evictions, he said, there were "no cliff edges here" and that the Duchy was working closely with every tenant to find a suitable outcome.

"In the main, our mission is to sell to our farmers. We are keen that wherever possible we can achieve that continuity," Morris explained.

"For many of our farmers, it's a generational aspiration to own their farm. A few people have said it to me: 'My grandfather wanted to buy his farm. My father wanted to buy the farm. And now I've got the opportunity and it's an amazing outcome'.

"That's kind of what's driving me through what, at times, has been a little bit of turbulence."

The Duchy - which was established in 1337 - currently has around 700 agricultural lettings, with around 300 whole farm holdings made up of a farmhouse, land and buildings.

Farmers are on a mix of contracts ranging from time-limited to lifelong, with an option to pass the tenancy down through a family.

George Dunn, TFA chief executive, said the organisation was in "deep discussions" with the Duchy and that poor communication had led to tenants "facing prolonged uncertainty over valuations, timing and the options available to them".

"Once a family is told that its long-term relationship with the Duchy may change permanently, that uncertainty lives with them 24/7," he told the BBC.

He added that while he welcomed the Duchy's assurance that "nobody will be made homeless" not every tenant "will be able or want to buy the farms that they operate and fair alternatives must be explored for those for whom ownership is unaffordable".

A spokeswoman for the Duchy said: "We are engaging with people directly and supporting them through the process with care and respect.

"We recognise that each of our tenant's circumstances are different, and we are taking a careful, case-by-case approach."

Sonia Gandhi has been one of the most powerful political figures in India's history

On the morning of 31 October 1984, Sonia Gandhi was a young wife and mother, living in the prime minister's residence in Delhi. She was about to take a bath when she heard shots ring out in the garden.

Her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, India's prime minister, had just left for her office in an adjoining building. Moments later, she would be assassinated by two of her Sikh bodyguards, in retaliation for the Indian army's storming of the Golden Temple in Amritsar, Sikhism's holiest shrine, earlier that year.

The sound was like firecrackers, but "different". The children's nanny came pounding on the bathroom door, hysterical, pointing towards the garden.

Sonia ran towards the path. A white Ambassador car was moving slowly towards her. Inside, Indira lay covered in blood, her sari stained, her eyes open, her face wearing what Sonia remembered as a look of surprise.

"Mummy, Mummy," she tried to say. No words came. At the hospital, she waited for hours before a doctor's shake of the head told her what she feared.

The ordeal did not end there. Rajiv Gandhi, her husband and the elder son of Indira Gandhi, summoned from a rally in West Bengal, arrived to tell her that party leaders wanted him to become prime minister.

Sonia's response was fury and terror. "They will kill you; they will kill you, too!" she pleaded. Rajiv replied: "They will kill me anyway." That evening, as Indira's body lay at home, Rajiv was sworn in.

It is one of the most searing passages in Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia Gandhi's new memoir: private devastation unfolding alongside the pressures of public life.

The woman who had largely stayed away from politics was now married to India's prime minister, and would eventually find herself at the head of the Congress party, leading it through two general election victories and becoming one of the country's most consequential political figures.

The passage also foreshadows another devastating loss. In 1991, Rajiv himself was assassinated.

Indira Gandhi was asssassinated by her Sikh bodyguards in October 1984

For Sonia, the years that followed were marked by retreat.

At 19, a young woman from a small Italian town, she had met Rajiv, an Indian student, in England. Their relationship took her into a new country and family, and a close bond with Indira followed. India became home through her husband and her mother-in-law.

After Rajiv's killing, even the public appearances required by the memorial trusts she headed became an ordeal. Before speeches, she feared tears would overwhelm her.

When the Dalai Lama asked whether she felt vengeful towards her husband's killers, she answered, "No, I don't," and burst into sobs. Slowly, she writes, Rajiv became "a presence within me rather than a piercing absence".

But grief returned at family milestones. At her son Rahul's Cambridge graduation in 1995, she and her children were overcome by the thought of how proud Rajiv would have been.

Politics, meanwhile, was closing in. The Congress party, the political vehicle of her husband's family for generations, was losing cohesion and electoral ground. Senior leaders were defecting, and the calls for Sonia to step in were growing louder.

She initially refused. She writes she had seen politics through Rajiv: its achievements, but also its "ambition and greed, hypocrisy and treachery". "I'd always disliked politics," she writes. It had taken first her mother-in-law, then "the love of my life, my children's father".

Yet the party's decline began to feel personal. Walking past photographs of Indira and Rajiv, she was seized by "a mixture of pain and guilt". She feared that the forces they had fought to "protect India's pluralistic ethos" were gaining ground: a rising Hindu nationalism that, in her view, threatened the "secular and pluralistic vision" of India they had sought to defend.

Congress leaders argued that without her, the party could splinter, leaving little to resist communal politics. The family name, she believed, carried an appeal beyond religion, caste, language and region. This, she says, was "the most compelling argument".

Rajiv Gandhi took oath as India's youngest prime minister hours after his mother's death

Her doubts were also about her own credentials. How could an outsider occupy a position held by two formidable figures? At home, Rahul and Priyanka feared losing their mother as they had lost their grandmother and father. Before a New Year holiday, they extracted a promise: "Don't you do anything crazy while we're away."

The "answer", she says, came through the Bhagavad Gita . Though not religious in adult life, Sonia arranged private lessons with a Sanskrit scholar in January 1997. They read the text verse by verse. She writes that its central message – to perform one's dharma, or duty, without attachment to the fruits of one's actions – eventually resolved her inner conflict.

"I had the answer to my own doubts and questions. I had to step out and go where my duty called. And I did."

The memoir's most dramatic political scene, however, comes seven years later, after Congress's 2004 election victory . Sonia had led the party's campaign.

Sonia goes with Manmohan Sing h to meet India's president at the presidential palace in Delhi and formally stake the Congress-led alliance's claim to form a government. Everyone assumes she will become prime minister. She says nothing.

At home, she tells a senior aide she intends to refuse. Party workers gather at the gates; senior colleagues demand a meeting.

"You fought the election, you led us," says one. "People believed in you. How can you let them down like this? Our workers will revolt. You think they'll accept another leader?"

Alliance leaders arrive to persuade her. They surround her, she recalls, and one insists: "We will not take no for an answer." Overwhelmed, she murmurs " Theek hai " - all right. They take it as consent and begin congratulating her.

Her children are appalled, she writes. Rahul storms in: "You said yes?" Her daughter Priyanka urges her not to be forced into a decision.

Sonia writes she spends a long night arguing with herself, friends and family. The risk is not merely personal. She believes the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) would continue to exploit her foreign birth and that accepting office would allow the controversy to "create havoc" and hurt the country. By morning she is clear. " I've made up my mind . I'm going to stick to my stand," she tells Rahul.

Sonia Gandhi (centre), with daughter Priyanka and son Rahul, at the funeral of Rajiv Gandhi in 1991

She chooses Singh, a trained economist and a party member, instead, describing him as a man "above reproach", with a "deep and consummate understanding of governance".

The book is at its most revealing when it turns from family memory to the India she believes has been lost.

Sonia says that when she entered public life there was "a certain decency and decorum in parliamentary politics".

Political attacks and harsh words were not new, but she sees a sharper appetite among those in power "to belittle and torment those who differ from them, to intimidate those they perceive as opponents". It is, she says, part of a wider international drift towards "a heartlessness that accompanies authoritarian regimes".

Her portrait of prime minister Narendra Modi of the Hindu nationalist BJP is unusually direct.

The two have had "practically no real contact", she writes, beyond formal greetings at parliamentary gatherings and occasional exchanges - " Theek hain, aap ?" ("Are you all right?") - when she returned from hospital. "He tends to look away," she says, "avoiding eye contact."

Sonia Gandhi with Manmohan Singh, whom she chose as prime minister after declining the post herself when Congress returned to power in 2004

Modi's idea of India, she writes, was shaped by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and "affirmed a fundamentalism in which his faith and culture superseded all others". His is an India of "hierarchy, order, and control"; hers is "an India against hegemony", standing for "inclusiveness, secularism, and social justice".

There is a striking concession amid the polemic - she says she understood Modi's "discomfort with the ruling elite of our times".

Sonia says she felt uneasy in Delhi's privileged drawing rooms, where political conversation seemed "very far removed from the reality of India".

Modi's origins, she writes, "may not be as humble as his PR team" suggests, but he "had certainly worked his way to power within the RSS from an underprivileged world". It is a rare acknowledgement of the social distance between the Congress establishment and the electorate Modi came to represent.

The memoir also offers some glimpses of Sonia's encounters with world leaders.

She remembers Vladimir Putin as an "engaging personality" who took her on a boat ride in St Petersburg, pointing out monuments along the way. She says she was impressed by his grasp of geopolitics and his "determination to restore Russia to its former powerful status" - "long before the Ukraine war, a different era".

Sonia Gandhi writes that she and PM Modi (foreground) have had "practically no real contact"

A more amusing encounter involved France's Nicolas Sarkozy, who arrived in India in 2008 without his then partner Carla Bruni because they were unmarried.

At a state banquet, the Indian vice-president's wife cheerfully grilled him about when he planned to marry her, whether he missed her and whether a date had been fixed. Sarkozy obligingly answered her questions while messaging Bruni on his phone.

Belonging is not a neutral history. The Bofors gun scandal, which badly damaged Rajiv Gandhi's government and dogged the family for decades, gets a relatively brief treatment.

The 502-page memoir is less forthcoming about the less flattering aspects of Congress's own record. Sonia has much to say about political corruption, hypocrisy and the decline of public standards under her opponents, but largely sidesteps the culture of patronage, cronyism and corruption that dogged Congress during its years in power. There is little reckoning, either, with the party's own share of responsibility for the erosion of public trust.

She is at pains to defend the political inheritance of her husband and mother-in-law, even as the party they built has suffered a prolonged decline. The story she tells is as much about the costs of carrying that inheritance as it is about a woman who says she never wanted the life she ended up leading.

That gives the memoir's final pages an unmistakable melancholy. Sonia, 79, is now a member of the Rajya Sabha, the upper house of parliament. Rahul, 55, is a four-term MP and leader of the opposition; Priyanka, 53, is also a member of parliament.

Sonia says the challenge was to remain faithful to "a just and humane society", through pain and loss, victory and defeat, and the manoeuvring that politics demands. But she ends not with triumph, nor even with the assurance that history will vindicate her.

"At this moment it seems to me that, although I tried my best, I didn't succeed in beating back the forces I'd set out to fight."

Watch: Vinícius Jr's surprise message to boy who received prosthetic legs after Sudan drone strike

In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.

The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger Vinícius Júnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.

Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.

We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.

More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.

Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.

More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.

In his video message, Real Madrid star Vinícius Jr invited Zaher to watch a Real Madrid match together

The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.

For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.

When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was Vinícius Júnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together.

"I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.

Vinícius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."

Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."

Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new Vinícius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer.

"Tell Vinícius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".

Zaher is one of millions of children whose lives have been devastated by Sudan's civil war

Zaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF.

Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets.

Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck.

"I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year.

She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer."

Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes.

Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection.

"I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to," he said at the time .

There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world.

Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising £45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care.

Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war.

Zaher has learned to use his new legs with months of support from doctors and physiotherapists in Cairo

After months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged.

For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive.

'I can't afford to save both twins': Sudan's war left one mother with an impossible choice

A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan

Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through.

"He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself."

His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them.

As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him.

He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home.

For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war.

Khartoum has suffered extensive damage, with many buildings damaged and their contents stolen

The state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted.

Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states. The group also warned of "potential famine" .

"I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries.

Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows.

Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs.

This South Korean vessel is among the ships damaged in the Strait of Hormuz

Traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most dangerous trips a vessel can take.

Despite assistance from the US Navy, ships are still being attacked .

"To transit the Strait of Hormuz you need agreement between the captain and the crew to take the risk. You need war risk insurance. And the captain has to make the final decision," says Steve Cameron, a former merchant navy officer and maritime consultant.

Missiles and drones are a threat from the air, but under the surface mines may also be lurking.

"If you're a captain, you'd like to see evidence mines aren't present," Cameron adds.

Modern mines rest on the seabed and detonate when they detect an acoustic or magnetic signal, triggering a pressure wave that will break the keel of a passing vessel.

Others can rise through shallow waters or float, or be powered towards a target.

The technology itself is not difficult or costly, but the mere threat can stop a tanker fleet from sailing.

Ian McFarlane of French defence group Thales is a naval architect who knows mine warfare well. "Mines are a very cheap way of waging a naval war, as the Royal Navy is acutely aware," he says.

Finding sea mines has traditionally been the job of specialist mine-hunting vessels, with crews of around 80 sailors.

To keep humans out of harm's way, an increasing amount of the work is done by systems that are autonomous and monitored from the shore.

They might only need 20 personnel, working in shifts on land. With the recruitment and retention challenges facing Nato navies these highly-portable robot systems are very attractive.

Such tech has been under development for 20 years.

During the 2003 Iraq war the US Navy poked around the seabed looking for mines with a torpedo-shaped robot called the Remus 100.

Pinging around with sonar these little machines operated down to around 100ft depth and spared divers a difficult and dangerous task.

Iran's military published this picture of a US submersible captured in the Gulf

The latest conflict in the Gulf is testing much more capable systems.

The US military is sparing with details about their mine-hunting craft, but we have seen glimpses of them.

Iranian forces hauled an uncrewed US autonomous sub , external out of the waters of the Strait of Hormuz in early September.

The Pentagon claimed this robot, an Extra Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV) from US autonomous defence tech venture Anduril, was a malfunctioning older device with no classified equipment on-board.

Whatever its mission, no sailors were imperilled. That, says William Lupton, a naval analyst with Shephard Group, "was a drop in the ocean compared to having prisoners taken", and part of the point of uncrewed vessels.

What if an uncrewed vessel is captured? Nato navies are reluctant to go into details, but computer drives can be wiped or destroyed remotely by various means. This may have taken place inside the humming circuit boards of the XLUUV seized by Iran.

The Thales Uncrewed Surface Vehicle is packed with sensors

Such autonomous tech is being embraced by forces around the world.

Cooperation between Thales, the Royal Navy, and France's Marine Nationale has produced a robot motor launch.

The Thales Uncrewed Surface Vehicle (USV) is packed with sensors programmed to detect mines via sonar that was developed for the oil and gas industries.

It tows a 5m long rectangular box, similar to a large torpedo, that takes a hi-resolution look at the seabed and creates a 3D picture refined by AI. The latest mines are designed to blend into their surroundings and the software spots anything that looks like a mine.

Autonomous systems are cheaper than conventional minehunters, plus they can be deployed, along with containerised control centres, by air.

Steve Prest, associate fellow at the RUSI defence think tank, introduced uncrewed mine hunting into the Royal Navy and was its first fleet robotics officer, a title he acquired in 2014.

"There is a bunch of ways to look for a mine using robot boats or robot subs, and while you can't prove the negative, that no mines are there, you can reduce the risk."

He says US robot minehunters can either blow up a mine or just mark the spot as somewhere to avoid.

"We'll see more use of autonomy but also the missions and capability will expand. And AI will be analysing data from those vessels on the spot as opposed to data being analysed when a drone returns."

The Royal Navy recently announced its concept of a hybrid navy - mixing drones with conventional warships. But Prest thinks for this vision to succeed the fleet must operate as one distributed force, sharing data in what he terms a cognitive architecture.

The robot only makes a real difference as part of this scheme and it's a mistake to focus on individual uncrewed assets. "Uncrewed or autonomous vessels are not the operating system. They are applications running on it."

Steve Prest introduced uncrewed mine hunting into the Royal Navy

While robots are on the rise, people are what really matter in the Strait.

Neil Roberts speaks for insurers at Lloyd's of London on marine matters and says the psychological impact of the mine threat is inescapable, as is the uncertainty around just how many mines, if any, are out there.

"The US says it has cleared the Omani route and believes the mine threat is being managed, with shipments running at about 75% of pre-conflict levels."

Fear of the unknown is the most potent aspect of the sea mine threat and robots are now the weapon of choice to confront that fear.
